summary: Describes architectural and operational problems that arise when link-layer protocols support more than one way of encapsulating IP. It argues for avoiding such multiplicity. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: If a road allows several ways to pack a package, senders and receivers may pick different ways and fail to understand each other. This note says that is a bad idea.

subtitle: Why link-layer protocols should not support multiple ways to wrap IP packets

tldr.problem: Link-layer protocols that support multiple ways of encapsulating IP packets (wrapping them in different headers) create interoperability and operational problems because not all hosts may support the same method.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes historical examples like Ethernet and traces how multiple encapsulations fragment the network into incompatible groups, examines arguments for supporting multiple methods, and shows that alternatives like compression or single encapsulations solve the same problems better.
tldr.outcome: The recommendation is that link-layer protocols should standardize on a single encapsulation method to avoid the complexity and fragmentation that multiple methods create.

today: RFC 4840 is an informational document from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) providing architectural guidance on link-layer design. It has not been obsoleted. The recommendation to use single encapsulations has been followed: for example, IPv6 transmission over Ethernet uses a single standardized method, learning from IPv4's experience.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Problem
sections.content:
Link-layer protocols sit just below IP and wrap IP packets for transmission over physical media like Ethernet cables or wireless links. Most protocols support just one way to do this wrapping, called an encapsulation method. But some protocols, including Ethernet, PPP, and IEEE 802.16, allow multiple methods on the same link.

When that happens, different computers may support different methods. A computer sending a packet via one method might send it to a receiver that only understands a different method, causing delivery failure. Even worse, broadcast packets intended for all computers on the link may only reach those using one particular method.

This document describes why this fragmentation occurs, examines historical attempts to live with it, and argues that supporting multiple encapsulations creates more problems than it solves.
sections.eli5: Some roads let packages be wrapped in multiple ways. When that happens, senders and receivers often pick different wrapping methods and fail to understand each other.

sections.title: Ethernet: The Cautionary Tale
sections.content:
Ethernet is the primary example. The protocol can encapsulate IP packets in three ways: the Ethernet (DIX) encapsulation defined in RFC 894, the IEEE 802.2/802.3 LLC encapsulation from RFC 1042, and the now-obsolete trailer encapsulation from RFC 893.

On a shared Ethernet cable, a computer might receive both DIX and IEEE 802 packets because different computers send using different methods. If the computer only supports one method for sending, it cannot initiate communication with computers using the other method. If a computer supports both for sending and receiving, it must track which method each peer uses—a complex and unreliable approach.

Broadcast packets sent using one encapsulation method do not reach computers configured to use the other, fragmenting the network into incompatible groups. Since most computers default to only one method, these groups cannot communicate directly.

RFC 1122 resolved this for Ethernet by making Ethernet (DIX) encapsulation mandatory for both send and receive, with IEEE 802 optional to receive, and making DIX the default for sending. This single dominant method eliminated the fragmentation problem.
sections.eli5: Ethernet used to allow three ways to wrap IP. Computers using different wrapping methods could not talk to each other, and broadcasts only reached computers using the same method. The solution was to make one method the required default, which worked.

sections.title: Architectural and Operational Problems
sections.content:
Multiple encapsulations create cascading problems beyond simple incompatibility. When different encapsulations coexist, they often have different Maximum Transfer Units (MTUs)—the largest packet size they can handle. DIX Ethernet supports 1500-byte IP packets, but IEEE 802.3 only supports 1492 bytes. If the link layer does not tell IP which MTU applies per destination, IP must use a single default MTU small enough to avoid fragmentation on any destination, reducing network efficiency.

Negotiation of encapsulation methods is also problematic. Negotiating above the link layer (e.g., in ARP or IP) requires sending negotiation packets over multiple encapsulation methods simultaneously to discover which the peer supports—expensive and unreliable. Link-layer negotiation (as Ethernet trailer negotiation attempted) works only when all hosts support certain baseline methods and is fragile when mixed with other encapsulations.

Service inconsistency arises in protocols like IEEE 802.16, which offers both raw IP encapsulation and Ethernet-framed encapsulation. Raw IP can map directly to link-layer quality-of-service (QoS) features, but Ethernet-framed packets must go through an intermediate translation layer that cannot use QoS the same way. An application might experience different performance depending on which encapsulation the system chose.

Implementation complexity increases dramatically. Devices with limited resources may be forced to support multiple encapsulations to interoperate, and hardware that requires specific encapsulation support may lead to market fragmentation where devices support different subsets of methods.
sections.eli5: Multiple wrapping methods cause packet-size mismatches, make it hard to discover which method peers use, can degrade service quality, and force devices to implement multiple incompatible systems instead of one.

sections.title: Why the Arguments for Multiple Encapsulations Fail
sections.content:
Proponents of multiple encapsulations offer three main arguments, but each has a stronger alternative.

Efficiency: The claim is that support for Ethernet encapsulation adds overhead that hurts performance on bandwidth-constrained links like wireless networks. However, link layers can achieve the same efficiency gain through header compression negotiated below the IP layer, without requiring multiple incompatible encapsulations. PPP's Compression Control Protocol (CCP) is a working example, allowing frame compression transparent to IP. Even wireless multicast efficiency improves more through selective unicast and rate negotiation than through creating a new encapsulation.

Multicast and broadcast: Some argue that certain link layers cannot efficiently distribute IP multicast and broadcast traffic, so alternatives are needed. But any link layer must support broadcast and multicast distribution by design—the RFC simply requires it be done consistently. Techniques like multicast snooping and the assignment of separate IP prefixes to hosts address the few real cases where efficiency is a problem.

Multiple uses: The claim that different deployment scenarios (wireless versus wired, fixed versus mobile) need different encapsulations assumes no single encapsulation is flexible enough. Yet PPP works in wireless (GPRS), wired (PPP over SONET), and bridged contexts. Ethernet works in wired networks and 802.11 WLANs. A single well-chosen encapsulation can cover disparate scenarios. The risk of choosing a new encapsulation is high: operating system integration becomes complex, and drivers may cut corners (e.g., supporting only IPv4, not IPv6) to reduce work, harming interoperability.
sections.eli5: People argue for multiple wrapping methods for efficiency, broadcast handling, and flexibility, but compression, proper broadcast design, and flexible single standards solve these problems better.

sections.title: The Path Forward
sections.content:
The RFC's recommendations are clear and practical. When developing new link-layer standards, only one IP encapsulation method should be standardized. If a link-layer technology already supports multiple methods (as Ethernet and IEEE 802.16 do), only one should be in use on any given link.

When multiple methods must coexist during a transition period, one must be mandatory to implement for both send and receive, and it must be the default for sending. This prevents the fragmentation that occurs when devices support different subsets.

Where efficiency concerns drive a desire for encapsulation alternatives, use header compression negotiated at the link layer instead. Where multicast or broadcast is difficult, address it with alternative distribution techniques (unicast replication, snooping, separate prefixes) rather than alternative encapsulations. Where new protocols need to run over a link layer, add support to the existing encapsulation rather than introducing a new encapsulation method.

These recommendations prioritize network simplicity, predictability, and interoperability over theoretical flexibility.
sections.eli5: New roads should pick one wrapping method. Old roads with multiple methods should use only one at a time. If efficiency is a problem, use compression, not a new wrapping method. This keeps networks simple and everything talking to everything else.
